analysis.one_liner: Lets seniors keep more earnings without losing Social Security, and eases federal penalties on small businesses.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 328-91 on March 28, 1996, cleared the Senate by unanimous consent the same day, and was signed into law by President Clinton on March 29, 1996.
analysis.plain_summary: This law raises the amount working retirees can earn before their Social Security benefits are reduced, phased up through 2002. It also creates the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act: plain-language compliance guides, an enforcement ombudsman, penalty reductions and waivers for small businesses, and a process letting Congress vote to cancel major federal rules. It denies disability benefits to people whose disability rests on drug addiction or alcoholism, funds substance-abuse treatment, and raises the federal debt limit to $5.5 trillion.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees who work: the yearly amount they can earn before losing benefits roughly doubles by 2002 (monthly exempt amounts rise from about $1,042 to $2,500). Small businesses get compliance guides, a regulatory enforcement ombudsman, penalty reduction and waiver programs, larger attorney-fee awards when agencies make excessive demands, and easier court challenges to rules. People with addiction-related disabilities can be referred to state treatment programs funded with $50 million a year in 1997 and 1998.

how_it_helps.text: Phases in much higher Social Security earnings limits for people at retirement age, from $1,041.67 per month in 1996-97 to $2,500 per month by 2002, so seniors can work without losing benefits.

Requires agencies to publish plain-language compliance guides for rules affecting small businesses and to answer small businesses' compliance questions [S3]. Creates a Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and regional fairness boards to review complaints about enforcement [S4].
Requires agencies to create programs to reduce and sometimes waive civil penalties for small businesses, excluding willful conduct and serious health or safety threats [S4].
Raises the attorney-fee rate awarded to small parties who prevail against the government from $75 to $125 an hour and requires fee awards when an agency's demand is substantially excessive [S4].
Lets small entities sue over agency failures to analyze a rule's effect on small business, and gives EPA and OSHA rules a special small-business review panel before proposals are published [S4].

Creates the Congressional Review Act: major rules with $100 million or more in annual economic effects are delayed 60 days, and Congress can pass a joint resolution to cancel a rule under expedited procedures [S4].
Appropriates $50 million a year for fiscal 1997 and 1998 to supplement state and tribal alcohol and drug treatment programs [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People whose disability is based on drug addiction or alcoholism lose Social Security disability and SSI benefits, though they can be referred to state treatment programs. Taxpayers bear the cost of the higher $5.5 trillion debt limit. The public bears weakened regulatory enforcement: agencies must offer penalty reductions and waivers to small violators, and Congress can cancel major rules. Social Security and Medicare trust funds finance continuing disability reviews designed to cut benefit rolls.

drawbacks.text: Denies disability benefits under Social Security and SSI to anyone whose drug addiction or alcoholism is a contributing factor material to the disability determination, cutting off income for a vulnerable group [S4].

The Congressional Review Act gives Congress expedited power to cancel major rules, which can block or delay public health, safety, and environmental protections once a hostile majority controls Congress [S4].

Penalty reduction and waiver programs let small entities avoid civil fines for regulatory violations in appropriate circumstances, reducing deterrence even for negligent conduct short of willful wrongdoing [S4].
Raises the public debt limit to $5.5 trillion, adding to future interest costs [S4].
Requiring disability reviews that 'maximize savings' directs agencies to cut benefit rolls, and tightens stepchild benefit rules to require actual dependency [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The earnings-limit increase is a genuine, broadly supported gain for working seniors, and plain-language compliance help for small businesses is low-risk. But the law pays for part of its agenda by cutting off disabled people whose addiction is a factor in their disability, and its regulatory provisions — penalty waivers, fee-shifting against agencies, and congressional veto of major rules — tilt enforcement toward regulated businesses in ways an honest supporter has to weigh against the public's protection from unsafe or unfair practices.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 328-91 on a bipartisan vote, the Senate passed it without changes by unanimous consent the same day, and President Clinton signed it the next day.

narrative.text: Introduced March 21, 1996 by Ways and Means Chairman Bill Archer and referred to six committees, the bill was brought to the floor under a special rule from the Rules Committee on March 28 [S6].
The House passed the bill 328-91 (Roll 102), with 201 of 235 voting Republicans and 127 of 195 voting Democrats in favor [S7].

Democratic attempts to recommit the bill with instructions failed: a motion by Minority Whip David Bonior failed to gain consideration 192-228 (Roll 100), and a motion by Rep. Orton failed 159-256 (Roll 101) [S6].
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by unanimous consent on March 28, 1996, and the President signed it March 29, making it Public Law 104-121 [S6].

The version as introduced contained a line-item veto title; the version that passed and became law instead contained the small business and congressional review provisions, with the debt limit increase retained [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working seniors keep more of their earnings, small businesses gained protections from federal penalties, and congressional Republicans and President Clinton each delivered a legislative priority. People with addiction-based disabilities lost benefits.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was broad and bipartisan (201 of 235 Republicans and 127 of 195 Democrats voted yes), but the Democratic motions to recommit split almost entirely by party, with only 7 Republicans supporting the Bonior motion and 13 the Orton motion.

industries.note: The law requires plain-language compliance guides, creates an enforcement ombudsman and regional fairness boards, and mandates penalty reduction and waiver programs for small violators. Most of this runs alongside ordinary people's interests, though weakened penalties also mean less deterrence against negligent violators.

Agencies must offer penalty waivers to small entities, face fee awards when their enforcement demands are excessive, and see major rules delayed and subject to congressional cancellation under the Congressional Review Act. Their interest in preserving enforcement authority ran against the bill's deregulatory thrust.
The law appropriates $50 million a year for fiscal 1997 and 1998 to supplement state and tribal alcohol and drug treatment programs, prioritizing treatment activities.

industries.industry: Brand-name and generic drug makers, and insurers
industries.note: Continuing disability review funding is designed to maximize savings in Medicare and Medicaid, trimming program spending that flows to providers and insurers, though this is an indirect and modest effect.
